t: Copper mining at Faynan and in the Timna Valley, dated to 1300–800 BCE, and the scale of the mines at Khirbat en-Nahas are read as evidence of a strong, centralized Edomite kingdom in the 10th century BCE.
Assyrian inscriptions name three kings of Edom, Kaus-malaka, Aya-ramu and Kaus-gabri, between about 745 and 680 BCE; the last unambiguous reference to Edom is an Assyrian inscription of 667 BCE.
After the fall of the kingdom in the 6th century BCE the Edomites settled in southern Judah, where they were known as Idumaeans; Herod the Great was of Edomite origin.
dyk: Qaus, the national god of Edom invoked in Edomite letters and personal names, is never mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, unlike the gods of other nearby nations; some scholars explain the silence by his close likeness to Yahweh.
ev: The earliest Iron Age settlements of Edom, possibly copper mining camps, are founded
Large-scale copper mining at Khirbat en-Nahas points to a strong, centralized Edomite kingdom
By the biblical account Amaziah of Judah defeats the Edomites and seizes Selah, their principal stronghold
Kaus-malaka, king of Edom, is named in Assyrian inscriptions of the time of Tiglath-pileser III
An Assyrian inscription makes the last unambiguous reference to Edom
Nebuchadnezzar II takes Jerusalem; the Edomites may have helped plunder the city, and their settlement in southern Judah is already under way
Nabonidus of Babylon conquers Edom, which ceases to exist as a state

f.capital: Bozrah (now Busaira, Jordan), by the Hebrew Bible; Selah its principal stronghold in the time of Amaziah of Judah
f.founder: Not known; Genesis 36 names Bela son of Beor as the first of the kings of Edom
f.predecessor: Nomadic groups of the region, possibly the Shasu of the Egyptian records; by the Book of Genesis the Horites, displaced by Esau's descendants
f.successor: Conquest by Nabonidus of Babylon; the Nabataean kingdom in the old land of Edom, and Idumaea in southern Judah, where the Edomites settled
